title: Planting forests
hook: Sikh groups plant small forests to honor Guru Nanak

segments.voice: Yesterday, cleaning a river, and your line was clean the river. Did you pick up something near water? Today the volunteers climb out of the river and pick up shovels. Day one thousand forty-two.

A scrap of land behind a village school. Hard dirt, a broken wall, a pile of bricks nobody moved. A sangat arrives after the Sunday program with saplings in plastic bags, a cart of compost, and a list of trees that belong to this soil. They don't plant in neat rows with space between. They plant close, shoulder to shoulder, the way a real forest grows. Children help press the earth down around each stem. A few seasons later, that scrap of dirt is a green wall full of birds. It was planted for one person. Today, planting forests.
screen: `A SCRAP OF HARD DIRT.` → `SAPLINGS SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` → `A GREEN WALL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. Sikh groups have been planting small, dense forests in honor of Guru Nanak, on patches of land near gurdwaras, schools, farms and villages. Some call them Guru Nanak sacred forests. Second, the method. Instead of a few big trees far apart, they plant native trees and shrubs close together, so they compete for light and grow fast and thick. Some groups use a way of planting that comes from Japan. The point is a real forest on a small plot, not a park. Third, the root. Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with a short salok, at Ang 8. In Gurmukhi it begins: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. So a forest isn't decoration. It's a family: air, water and earth, the ones the Guru named as teacher and parents. Fourth, the old green thread. Tradition remembers Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, keeping gardens and growing healing herbs, and tells of him as a boy brushing a flower with his robe and breaking it, and taking care with every living thing after that. The forests carry that thread forward. A tree planted for Nanak gives shade to anyone, of any faith, who sits under it. That's today's line: a forest for nanak. It honors the Guru by giving the earth, the great mother of the salok, back a little of what was taken.
screen: `SMALL FORESTS FOR GURU NANAK.` · `NATIVE TREES, PLANTED CLOSE.` · `AIR GURU, WATER FATHER, EARTH MOTHER.` · `GURU HAR RAI'S GARDENS.` · then, large: `A FOREST FOR NANAK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three the Guru named. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Breathe in, and notice the air: the Guru, the salok says. Feel your feet on the floor, and below the floor the earth: the great mother. Think of the water inside you, in every cell: the father. Air, water, earth. Stay with whichever one is easiest to feel. If you pray, you can say pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat once, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Planting forests. Sikh groups planting small, dense forests of native trees to honor Guru Nanak, who named air as Guru, water as father and earth as the great mother. Today's word.
Your line: a forest for nanak. Today, plant or water something: a seed in a pot, a houseplant that's been ignored, a street tree in a dry week. Day one thousand forty-two.

notes: The Japji closing salok is given in transliteration with a paraphrased meaning; please confirm Ang 8 and the Gurmukhi spelling ਧਰਤਿ in the original game.

'Some call them Guru Nanak sacred forests' and 'a way of planting first worked out in Japan' (the Miyawaki method) are given without names, counts or dates; please confirm. The organization (e.g. EcoSikh) is not named on purpose.
'Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with a short salok' describes the text's structure; confirm the phrasing.
Guru Har Rai's gardens, herbs and the flower story are framed as tradition; please confirm. 'The seventh Guru' is an ordinal the tradition itself gives.
The practice offers the salok's Gurmukhi line 'if you pray'; confirm it is suitable to recite this way.

Editor pass: 'a way of planting first worked out in Japan' became 'a way of planting that comes from Japan' (no unsourced 'first'); the hook's 'a group of volunteers' became a sangat after the Sunday program, so it doesn't echo day 1041's line of volunteers.

Audit pass: the Guru Har Rai flower story now follows the usual telling (he broke a flower with his robe as a boy and was careful ever after), not 'taking care not to break even a flower'. The closing line no longer says outright that Guru Nanak authored the Japji's closing salok, since a near-identical salok appears at Ang 146 under Guru Angad's name; Keeper to confirm preferred attribution.
